review: adversarial review of a625b64..60891da (demand tracking + AIS ships)
method: 4 lane reviewers, each verified by an independent skeptic told to refute

findings.summary: The region job counts a limiter `Throttled` (no request was sent) as a provider failure. After 3 of them, `ProviderChain.record_failure` puts the provider in a 600 s cooldown. A single 429 on a lower-priority focus/hot call can therefore take the fixed region offline for about 10 minutes.
findings.failure_scenario: adsb.lol is down or rate-limiting, so the region chain has fallen back to adsb_fi. A hot or focus call to opendata.adsb.fi gets HTTP 429, and HttpClient calls `limiter.penalize` (30 s). The next three 10 s region cycles hit `cooldown_remaining > REGION_WAIT_S (5 s)`, so `acquire` raises `Throttled` right away. `_on_fetch_error` releases the budget, but then reaches `elif self.chain.record_failure(name)` (http_status is None). The 3rd throttle marks adsb_fi down for 600 s, and `pick()` returns None while adsb.lol is still in its own 600 s cooldown. The region feed goes empty and `ctx.status.failure` reports adsb_fi as failing, although no call was made. Meanwhile focus/hot keep using adsb.fi after the 30 s penalty. This inverts the contracted priority (region > focus > hot). I reproduced it with the real `default_limiter`, `HttpClient` and `ProviderChain`: after `penalize` plus 3 `run_once`, adsb_fi was down for 600 s and `pick` returned None.
findings.suggested_fix: Handle `Throttled` separately in `_on_fetch_error`: release the budget, but do not call `record_failure` or `status.failure`. At most, skip the provider for `limiter.cooldown_remaining(host)` seconds. Keep 3-strike cooldowns for real provider errors only.
findings.evidence: Traced and reproduced. The region provider calls `_http.get(..., priority=PRIORITY_FIXED, wait_s=REGION_WAIT_S=5.0)` (providers/readsb.py:23,65). `RateLimiter.acquire` raises `Throttled` straight away when `cooldown_remaining(host) > wait_s` (ratelimit.py:144-147), and no request is sent. `HttpClient._request` penalizes the whole host on any 429, whichever caller got it (http.py:108-109; the first step is 30 s, ratelimit.py:30). In `AircraftJob._on_fetch_error` (jobs/aircraft.py:162-175), `Throttled` releases the budget but still calls `status.failure`. Because `http_status` is None, it then falls into `elif self.chain.record_failure(name)` at line 172, and 3 strikes mean `mark_down(600 s)` (fallback.py:85-93). `_fails` is reset only by `record_success`. The region chain order is adsb_lol,adsb_fi,opensky (config.py:27), and opensky has `supports_region=False` (providers/opensky.py:23), so `pick` returns None when both readsb providers are down. Probe (scratchpad review2/test_probe_c0.py) used the real `RateLimiter`/`HttpClient`/`ProviderChain`/`adsb_fi()` with a fake clock and adsb_lol marked down. I ran `penalize('opendata.adsb.fi')` (30 s), then region `run_once` at +1/+11/+21 s (cooldown 29/19/9 s, all > 5). Result: fails 1→2→cooldown, adsb_fi down_until ≈ now+600 s, `pick()` → None, provider hash `consecutive_failures=3`, and last_error shows the throttle. Nothing in DemandTracker consults the region chain, so focus/hot resume after the 30 s limiter penalty. Precondition: a single 30 s penalty gives 3 strikes only when the first region cycle lands within 5 s of the 429 (about half the time). A second 429 within 15 min (60 s penalty) always produces ≥3 strikes. A 429 on the region call itself only costs a 60 s chain backoff (fallback.py:76-83), so a 429 on a lower-priority call punishes the region harder than one on its own call. This matters only while the region is on the adsb_fi fallback, but that is exactly when the region depends on it.

findings.summary: The provider-clock reference is accepted when it is within ±120 s of the local receive time. The quality gate, however, rejects anything more than 30 s in the future, and the api drops focus observations older than 60 s. A 30–120 s clock offset therefore makes all readsb aircraft vanish instead of falling back to `fetched_at`.
findings.failure_scenario: The collector container's clock is 30–120 s behind the provider (for example, Docker Desktop VM clock drift after the Mac sleeps), or the provider clock is that far ahead. `readsb_reference_time` still returns `ref = now`, so `seen_at = ref - seen_pos` lies 30–120 s in the future. `AircraftGate._check` then quarantines every region, focus and hot record as `seen_in_future`, and the map empties. In my probe, skews of 45, 90 and 119 s were all quarantined, while 125 s was kept because it falls back. In the opposite direction (provider 60–120 s behind), every seen_at is aged by that offset. The api's `SnapshotStore.FOCUS_TTL_S=60` then drops focus observations on arrival. Before commit 964b31a, seen_at came from the local clock and these offsets had no effect.
findings.suggested_fix: Only use the provider `now` when it is within a small window of `fetched_at`, for example `fetched_at - 10 s <= ref <= fetched_at + 2 s`. The window must stay well inside `FUTURE_TOLERANCE_S` and the api TTLs. Otherwise fall back to `fetched_at`, and count or log the fallback.
findings.evidence: normalize.py:78,92 accepts the payload `now` as the reference when |ref - fetched_at| <= 120 s. `normalize_readsb` then sets `seen_at = ref - seen_pos` (normalize.py:110). `AircraftGate._check` quarantines when `-age > FUTURE_TOLERANCE_S = 30` (quality.py:23,86-88), with age measured against the local `datetime.now(UTC)` (aircraft.py:94, demand.py:324). Probe (review2/test_probe_c1.py, seen_pos 1.2 s): skew +20 was kept, while +45, +90 and +119 were all `seen_in_future`. +125 was kept because it falls back to fetched_at. Skew −45/−90 was kept but with an age of 46/91 s. api `SnapshotStore.FOCUS_TTL_S=60` expires focus entries at seen_at+60 s (SnapshotStore.java:37,51), so the −90 s case drops focus on arrival. The 120 s sanity window is therefore larger than the downstream 30 s future tolerance, and inside that band the fallback never fires while every readsb record (region, hot and focus) is quarantined. I lowered the severity for two reasons. First, the failure needs an abnormal clock offset of more than 30 s between the collector VM and adsb.lol/adsb.fi, which is plausible only with Docker Desktop VM drift, not in normal NTP-synced operation. Second, the pre-existing OpenSky path (seen_at from provider `time_position`, normalize.py:179-183) and AIS `time_utc` already rely on the same clock agreement against the same 30 s gate. The real defect is the mis-sized window.

findings.summary: `DemandTracker` never checks the operator's provider kill switch (`wakeline:provider:adsb_fi` disabled=1, set by POST /ops/providers/adsb_fi/disable). Focus (5 s) and hot (30 s) calls to opendata.adsb.fi continue after an operator disables adsb_fi.
findings.failure_scenario: An operator disables adsb_fi in the ops console, for example after a complaint or a 429 storm. `ProviderChain.pick` honours `status.is_disabled`, so the region job stops using adsb.fi. `DemandTracker._fetch` goes straight to budget reserve and `provider.fetch_icao/fetch_point` without checking the flag. Neither the api's DemandService nor the lease writer gates on it either. As long as any viewer has an aircraft selected or is zoomed in outside the region, the collector keeps sending up to about 0.4 req/s to adsb.fi, while the ops page shows the provider as disabled. Probe: with `hset wakeline:provider:adsb_fi disabled 1` and one focus lease, `is_disabled` returned True and the tracker still made `('icao', ['abcdef'], 4.0)`.
findings.suggested_fix: At the start of each tick, or in `_fetch`, call `await self.ctx.status.is_disabled(self.provider.name)`. If it is disabled, make no calls and write focus/hot status `throttled` with last_error "provider disabled by operator", so the UI states it honestly.
findings.evidence: The only consumer of `ProviderStatus.is_disabled` is `ProviderChain.pick` (fallback.py:58), confirmed by grep across wakeline_collector. `DemandTracker.tick` → `_schedule_focus`/`_schedule_hot` → `_run_focus`/`_run_hot` → `_fetch` (jobs/demand.py:169-176, 207-240, 277-300) goes straight to `budget.reserve` and `provider.fetch_icao`/`fetch_point` with no disabled check. main.py wires `DemandTracker(..., AdsbFiDemandProvider(http), ...)` and gates it only on `settings.demand_enabled`, which needs a restart to change. On the api side, DemandService and the demand/* classes do not read `wakeline:provider:*`; the only readers are OpsController (writing the flag) and StatusService (display). OpsController.toggleProvider accepts adsb_fi (StatusService.PROVIDERS), and ops/page.tsx:85 shows a 'disabled' badge. Before this diff, the region chain was the only adsb.fi caller, so disabling adsb_fi stopped all adsb.fi traffic. After it, focus (1 req / 5 s) and hot (up to 6 cells / 30 s) keep calling opendata.adsb.fi, roughly 0.4 req/s, while ops shows the provider as disabled. Mitigating context: the limiter and budget still cap the rate, and the awc/rainviewer/kma_radar disable flags were already no-ops before this diff. Even so, the new code removes a working operator control over adsb.fi traffic.

findings.summary: In `_pump`, a waiter whose host is in 429 cooldown still marks the global bucket as blocked when the bucket is momentarily short. The wake timer is then set to that waiter's cooldown end rather than the bucket refill time. Calls to unrelated hosts stall behind it and can be `Throttled` even though global tokens are available.
findings.failure_scenario: The global bucket was just drained by two calls (burst 2). A priority-0 waiter W1 for opendata.adsb.fi arrives with 3 s of cooldown left (<= its wait_s), and `_pump` puts `id(global)` in `blocked` because the global wait is about 0.5 s. W2 for api.adsb.lol (wait_s 2 s) is skipped because of that entry, and `next_wake` = W1's 3 s cooldown. W2 times out with `Throttled('no slot within 2.0 s')` while the global bucket has had 2 tokens since t≈0.5 s (reproduced with `RateLimiter(2.0, 2, {...})`). In the default configuration the typical effect is a delay of up to the head waiter's wait_s (5–10 s) for AWC/RainViewer/KMA/OpenSky calls. A region adsb.lol call behind such a head can be throttled outright.
findings.suggested_fix: When `cool > 0`, add only the host to `blocked_hosts` and do not reserve that waiter's buckets. Alternatively, set `next_wake` to include the refill time of each bucket a waiter marks as blocked (`min(s for s in waits if s > 0)`), so waiters behind it are re-examined as soon as tokens return.
findings.evidence: In ratelimit.py:197-211, a waiter whose host is in cooldown (`cool > 0`) still adds every bucket with `s > 0` to `blocked`, and `next_wake = need = max(waits + [cool])`, which is the cooldown end rather than the bucket refill time. Later waiters for other hosts that share the global bucket are skipped (line 194) until the next `_pump`. That next pump comes only from a new `acquire`, a `_drop`, or the timer. Acquires for a host in long cooldown raise `Throttled` before `_pump` (lines 144-147), so they do not trigger one. Probe (review2/test_probe_c3.py, real `RateLimiter(2.0, 2, {...})`): I drained the global bucket with 2 calls, gave opendata.adsb.fi 3 s of cooldown, queued W1 (adsb.fi, prio 0, wait 5 s), then W2 (api.adsb.lol, prio 0, wait 2 s). W2 was throttled at 2.0 s with 'no slot within 2.0 s' and W1 was granted at 3.0 s. The global bucket had refilled by about 0.5 s, and letting W2 through would not have delayed W1. In the default config the impact is narrow. Priority-1/2 waiters are all adsb.fi and therefore host-blocked anyway, so only a priority-0 waiter at the tail of a 429 penalty, arriving while the global bucket is momentarily empty, can stall other hosts for up to its remaining cooldown (≤ 5-10 s). A region adsb.lol call (5 s) is throttled only when that cooldown exceeds 5 s, and via claim #0 the throttle then counts as a chain strike. This is rare and its effect is small.

findings.summary: The reader calls feed.on_message() for every frame, including provider error frames such as {"error": ...}. The first error frame of a new session therefore counts as the "first message" and closes the open gap as if the feed had recovered. It also refreshes last_msg_at and msgs_total. This contradicts feed.py's own rule that a wrong-key connect/disconnect loop must not be recorded as recovery.
findings.failure_scenario: The aisstream key is revoked or the connection limit is exceeded, so every connect gets {"error":"Api Key Is Not Valid"} (the string the repo's own tests use) and then a close. Each attempt, about every 60-72 s at the backoff cap, runs: error frame -> on_message -> gaps.close(now) -> an ais_gap {started_at, ended_at} is XADDed and stored permanently in ingest_gap -> the disconnect reopens a new gap at the error-frame time. One real outage becomes a chain of about 1,400 per day 'ended' gaps, each claiming a recovery that never happened. The UI status bar shows 'AIS 공백 hh:mm–hh:mm' as ended. status.sources.ais.last_msg_at and msgs_per_s report a recent 'message' although no AIS data arrived. Reproduced locally against a loopback fake server: 15 sessions (1 data, 14 error-only) produced 14 closed gap events.
findings.suggested_fix: Do not treat provider error frames as data. Either cheaply detect {"error":...} frames in _read and skip on_message, or move gap close and first-message bookkeeping to the worker so it fires only after parse_message returns a position or static part.
findings.evidence: client.py:189-192 calls put(msg) and then on_message(wall()) for every frame with no inspection, so a {"error":...} frame goes through the same path as data. feed.py:131-139: the first on_message of a session sets _session_first, changes state to 'receiving', calls gaps.close(now) and bumps msgs_total and last_msg_at. The worker only later recognises the frame as provider_error (parse.py:251-253, worker.py:55-56), after the gap has already closed. The following disconnect runs feed.py:149-150, which reopens a gap at last_msg_at, i.e. the error-frame time. I simulated this with FeedState directly (scratchpad review2/v0.py): 1 data session then 5 error-then-close sessions left 5 closed gap events in gaps.pending, each started_at equal to the previous error-frame time. It is also worse than claimed: with a key that never worked and no earlier state, 3 error-only sessions still produced 2 closed gaps plus 1 open gap. That breaks feed.py:5-6 ('no data ever received -> no gap') as well as lines 7-8 ('a wrong-key loop is not recorded as recovery'). healthy stays about 0, so the backoff never resets (backoff.py:39-44). At the 60 s ±20% cap that is roughly 1,200-1,800 gap rows a day, each with a distinct started_at, so UNIQUE(source, started_at) keeps them all permanently in ingest_gap. gap_open_since also restarts about every minute, so the status bar understates how long the outage has lasted. The repo's own test test_ais_server.py:346 (msgs_total >= 81 = 80 data frames + 1 error frame) shows error frames are counted as messages. Medium is appropriate: permanent false records plus a misleading live status.

findings.summary: position_source is set to "gnss" for Timestamp 60, which USCG/ITU-R M.1371 defines as 'time stamp not available (default)', not a normal EPFS report. It is also set to "gnss" when Timestamp is missing, non-integer or out of range. In each case the report never said the position came from GNSS. The docstring (line 5) wrongly describes 0-60 as a normal electronic fix.
findings.failure_scenario: In the bundled real fixture, 10 of 428 position reports carry Timestamp 60. They are published as position_source "gnss" and the ship card shows '위치 출처: GNSS(선박 보고)', a source the ship never reported. A message with no Timestamp field is also labelled GNSS.
findings.suggested_fix: Map only 0-59 to "gnss". For 60, missing or invalid values, publish null, with a schema/contract update to allow null, so the card shows '—'.
findings.evidence: parse.py:295: POSITION_SOURCE.get(ts, 'gnss') maps 60 (and any value outside 61-63) to 'gnss', and a missing Timestamp also gives 'gnss'. The bundled real fixture has 428 position reports; 10 carry Timestamp 60 and none lack the field (counted from fixtures/ais_east_asia_90s.jsonl). The value goes through the api unchanged; web lib/ships.ts:309 labels it 'GNSS(선박 보고)' and ShipCard.tsx:80 shows it under '위치 출처'. In ITU-R M.1371 / NAVCEN, 60 means 'time stamp not available (default)' and says nothing about the fix source, so the parse.py:5 docstring and the ship_state.v1.json description ('0-60 = 정상 보고') are wrong about 60. Caveat: change-contract-v2.md:47 explicitly specifies 'else gnss', and V5__ships.sql:36 has position_source NOT NULL with a CHECK. The fix therefore needs a contract, schema and migration change, not only a parser change. The missing-Timestamp branch does not occur with aisstream (0 of 428), so the real impact is limited to the Timestamp 60 case, about 2% of reports.

findings.summary: _imo accepts 1,000,000-1,073,741,823 into the single `imo` field. Per the USCG/ITU table (quoted in ship_static.v1.json), values of 10,000,000 and above are official flag-state numbers, not IMO numbers. ShipCard still renders the field under the label 'IMO'.
findings.failure_scenario: A vessel whose message 5 carries 12345678 (a flag-state official number) appears in the ship card as 'IMO 12345678'. The value is mislabelled as an IMO number.
findings.suggested_fix: Publish only 1,000,000-9,999,999 as imo and set values of 10,000,000 and above to null (or a separate flag_state_no field). Alternatively, have the card label values of 10,000,000 and above as a flag-state number.
findings.evidence: parse.py:59/205 accepts 1,000,000-1,073,741,823 into imo. The repo's own ship_static.v1.json describes imo as '1,000,000-9,999,999 = IMO 번호, 10,000,000 이상 = 기국 공식 번호'. The api passes it through unchanged (ShipCodec.java:25, WsMessages.java:156). web parseShipStatic keeps it (lib/ships.ts:176, int 1..999,999,999), and ShipCard.tsx:76 renders any value under the label 'IMO' without distinguishing the flag-state range. So 12345678 would be shown as IMO 12345678. The actual mislabel is in ShipCard.tsx:76 rather than parse.py, where the collector matches its documented schema. No value of 10,000,000 or more appears in the fixture's 48 message-5 records, so this is a real but infrequent display mislabel.

findings.summary: For message 24 part B, the parser always takes Dimension as ship size. For auxiliary craft (MMSI 98MIDxxxx), ITU-R M.1371 uses those 30 bits for the mother ship's MMSI. The aisstream decoder exposes no mothership field (see the fixture's ReportB keys), so the published dim_a..dim_d values are fragments of an MMSI.
findings.failure_scenario: A tender with MMSI 984401234 sends 24B carrying its mother ship's MMSI. The decoder splits those bits into A/B/C/D, for example 400/20/50/30. The ship card then shows '크기 420 × 80 m · 보고값' for a small boat, with the invented size labelled as a reported value.
findings.suggested_fix: In _static, when the part-B MMSI starts with "98", set dim_a..dim_d to null (keep call_sign and ship_type).
findings.evidence: parse.py:317-327: for StaticDataReport PartNumber=true the parser always takes ReportB.Dimension, with no check on the MMSI prefix, and nothing in apps/ handles 98MID auxiliary craft (git grep found no matches). The fixture's ReportB keys are CallSign, Dimension, FixType, ShipType, Spare, Valid, VenderIDModel, VenderIDSerial and VendorIDName, so the decoder exposes no mothership-MMSI field. In ITU-R M.1371, those 30 bits carry the mother ship's MMSI for auxiliary craft. I simulated 24B from 984401234 with mother ship 440123456 split into its 9/9/6/6-bit fields: parse_message published dim_a=209, dim_b=444, dim_c=1, dim_d=0. All pass the _dims ranges and the web's dim_c/dim_d 0-63 clamp, so fmtShipSize would show '653 × 1 m · 보고값' for a small tender. The spec semantics are from my own knowledge of M.1371 (not checked online here). This needs auxiliary craft that transmit 24B, which are rare.

findings.summary: Shutdown waits only 1 s for sink_task, then runs sink.final() while sink_task may still be inside publish_gaps, flush or write_status. Both coroutines read pending[0] and each calls popleft() after its XADD (sink.py 153/169). The second pop removes an unsent gap event, or raises IndexError. A still-in-flight HSET from the old task can also land after the final 'stopped' status.
findings.failure_scenario: On SIGTERM shortly after a gap closed, with Redis slow (redis-py's default retries or an AOF fsync stall make one XADD take more than 1 s), sink_task and final() both XADD the same ais_gap. With 2 or more events pending, the second popleft drops the next gap event, which is never published and permanently missing from ingest_gap. With 1 pending, popleft raises IndexError. The IndexError is not caught (only TimeoutError is), so main exits with a traceback and never writes the final stopped status.
findings.suggested_fix: Cancel and await sink_task before calling final() (asyncio.wait -> cancel -> gather). Or make publish_gaps pop the event it actually sent, for example by popping before the XADD and pushing it back with appendleft on failure, under an asyncio.Lock shared with final().
findings.evidence: main.py:149: asyncio.wait([sink_task], timeout=1.0) does not cancel sink_task, and main.py:152 then runs sink.final() concurrently. Both reach publish_gaps (sink.py:152-169), which reads pending[0], awaits XADD and then calls popleft() with no lock. The trigger is realistic: redis-py 8.1.0 here defaults to Retry(ExponentialWithJitterBackoff(base=0.01, cap=1), 10 retries) on ConnectionError/TimeoutError, so one XADD during a Redis blip can easily take more than 1 s. I simulated this with the real AisSink and a stalled Redis stub that recovers 0.3 s into final(), reproducing the main.py:149-152 sequence (scratchpad review2/v4.py). With 1, 2 and 3 pending gaps, sink_task was still running after the 1 s wait, and final() raised IndexError('pop from an empty deque') every time. main catches only TimeoutError (main.py:153), so the IndexError leaves main() and asyncio.run with a traceback and nonzero exit, skipping final()'s flush of the last ship window. Two parts of the claim are overstated. Gap events were not lost: every distinct event was XADDed, with one duplicate that UNIQUE(source, started_at) absorbs. The element the second popleft removes is the one the other coroutine is sending at that moment, so an event is lost only if that XADD then fails or is cancelled before it is written. Also, the 'stopped' status was still written, by sink_task's own loop, because on_stopped sets changed. Remaining impact: a shutdown traceback and a possibly missing final flush in a narrow Redis-stall-at-SIGTERM window.

findings.summary: Ship static upserts go through a JDBC batch using `INSERT ... VALUES ... ON CONFLICT (mmsi) DO UPDATE`. With `reWriteBatchedInserts=true`, pgjdbc merges that batch into multi-row INSERTs of up to 128 rows. ShipWriter.write never dedupes `stats` by MMSI, so two static updates for one MMSI in the same block fail with SQLSTATE 21000. TrackWriter.isPermanent treats 21000 as transient, so ShipWriter retries the same failing batch forever and all ship persistence stops.
findings.failure_scenario:
1. ShipWriter.next() takes up to 2,000 queued items spanning several `ships` messages. This happens after an api restart (PEL plus up to about 33 min of stream backlog replayed in a burst), after a DB hiccup (the retry backoff lets messages pile up), or routinely at global-subscription volume.
2. A class-B ship sent AIS 24A (name) in flush N and 24B (call sign/type) in flush N+k. The collector publishes two statics for MMSI X with updated_at U1 < U2.
3. ShipWriter.select lets both through (U2 is after U1), and write() puts both rows in `stats`.
4. Both rows land in one rewritten VALUES block. I checked with the cached postgresql-42.7.13.jar Parser: STATIC_SQL and TOUCH_SQL are rewrite-compatible, POSITION_SQL is not.
5. PostgreSQL raises 21000, 'ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE command cannot affect row a second time'.
6. isPermanent only matches 22/23/42 and isTransient does not match 21000, so the loop retries the same `pending` batch with 2→30 s backoff indefinitely. Because upsertStatics runs first in write(), writePositions and touch never run either.
7. The queue fills to 100k and drops rows. Receipts beyond 1,000 marks are force-released, so messages are ACKed without being stored.
8. A restart replays the still-pending messages and can wedge again. The DB tests call upsertStatics with one row at a time, so they don't catch this.
findings.suggested_fix: In ShipWriter.write (or ShipRepository.upsertStatics), collapse `stats` to one row per MMSI, keeping the newest updated_at and the min/max receivedAt, before the batch runs. Also treat SQLState class 21 as permanent in TrackWriter.isPermanent, so one bad batch can never wedge the writer. Add a DB test with two statics for the same MMSI in one upsertStatics call while reWriteBatchedInserts is on.
findings.evidence: I traced every link in the chain. (1) application.yml:17 and DbTestSupport:153 set reWriteBatchedInserts=true. I ran org.postgresql.core.Parser.parseJdbcSql from the cached postgresql-42.7.13.jar on STATIC_SQL and TOUCH_SQL, and both return isBatchedReWriteCompatible()=true (the scratch harness is in scratchpad/review2/pg/P.java). With 19 binds per row, pgjdbc groups up to 128 consecutive rows into one multi-row INSERT. (2) ReceiptBatchQueue.take() drains up to BATCH=2000 items across message boundaries, so a batch covers several messages whenever the queue has backed up. That happens after an api restart, because StreamConsumer reads ReadOffset.lastConsumed() (line 425) and replays PEL plus backlog in a burst, and it happens after any retry/backoff period. (3) ShipWriter.select (lines 132-136) passes a second static for the same MMSI whenever updatedAt is strictly newer. On the collector side, ais/book.py apply_static sets a new static_at on every merged change: class-B 24A and 24B arriving in different 10 s flushes, destination or ETA edits, and buoys or shared MMSIs. So consecutive `ships` messages legitimately carry the same MMSI with U1<U2. (4) ShipWriter.write (lines 238-247) never dedupes `stats`. upsertStatics (ShipRepository:115) sends both rows, which then sit in one VALUES block. PostgreSQL raises 21000 ('ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE command cannot affect row a second time') in ExecOnConflictUpdate, before the DO UPDATE WHERE is evaluated, whenever the first row inserted or updated the tuple. (5) pgjdbc's BatchUpdateException keeps SQLState 21000. OrderedWriter.isTransient (lines 224-235) and TrackWriter.isPermanent (lines 395-404, which accepts only 22/23/42) both return false, so ShipWriter.loop (lines 212-228) retries the same `pending` forever with a 2→30 s backoff. upsertStatics runs first, so positions and touch never run either. The queue grows to QUEUE_MAX=100k and drops rows; beyond MAX_MARKS=1000, receipts are force-released and messages are ACKed without being stored. On shutdown, flush() writes `pending` first, fails, and writes nothing else. On restart, the unACKed pair is replayed with an empty staticSeen, which can wedge the writer again. ShipPersistDbTest:85-86 only ever calls upsertStatics with one row per call. touch() is safe because it dedupes through a map, and POSITION_SQL (INSERT...SELECT) is not rewritten.

findings.summary: The api is the only gatekeeper of demand leases, but nothing limits how often one session's focus hex or hot cell can change. Every select/subscribe produces a new lease set after the 1 s debounce. The collector fast-paths new ('fresh') focus hexes at a 2 s minimum gap (vs the 5 s cadence) and fetches new hot cells immediately. So one anonymous client can push adsb.fi usage well above the normal ~0.2 req/s and burn the daily budget for all users.
findings.failure_scenario:
1. A public web client, staying under the 20 msgs/10 s WS limit, alternates {type:'select', hex:A} / {type:'select', hex:B} about once per second.
2. DemandService.requestRefresh (1 s debounce) rewrites wakeline:demand:focus each second, and the new hex always fits under the 50-hex cap.
3. Collector DemandTracker._schedule_focus sees `fresh` hexes and issues an adsb.fi /v2/icao request every FOCUS_MIN_GAP_S = 2 s: 0.5 req/s, or about 43,200/day, against budget_adsb_fi = 40,000 with 8,640 reserved for the region.
4. Up to 4 more sessions from the same IP churning subscribe centres make new hot cells (_Cell(next_due=now)) that fire immediately, up to the 0.8 req/s bucket.
5. Within roughly 11–17 h the focus/hot share of the daily budget is gone. Every user's focus and hot-region tracking then reports throttled/'daily budget share exhausted' until 00:00 UTC.
6. The per-host rate cap still holds; the damage is budget exhaustion and denial of the feature to everyone else.
findings.suggested_fix: Rate-limit demand changes per session on the server. For example, require a new focus hex or hot cell to persist across at least one 10 s refresh before it is leased, or cap how many new keys one session may introduce per minute (ignore or delay further changes). Alternatively, stop the collector's fresh-hex fast path from firing more often than FOCUS_INTERVAL_S when the set is churning.
findings.evidence: The mechanism holds end to end. WakelineWsHandler.select (lines 157-176) accepts any 6-hex string (no check that the aircraft exists) and calls hub.demandChanged(). Only the per-session 20 msgs/10 s limit applies (WsSession:33-34), plus 5 connections per IP (application.yml:70). DemandService.requestRefresh (line 166) debounces for 1 s and then rewrites the leases. Nothing ties a lease to how long the key has persisted or to a per-session change rate. On the collector side, jobs/demand.py _schedule_focus (lines 207-217) fires as soon as any hex is 'fresh' and FOCUS_MIN_GAP_S=2.0 has elapsed, so alternating A/B gives one /v2/icao call every 2 s: 0.5 req/s instead of the 0.2 req/s that ADR-013 states ('묶음 요청은 대상 수와 무관하게 0.2 req/s'). In _schedule_hot (lines 219-240), every new cell key gets _Cell(next_due=now) and fires at once, bypassing the 30/60/120 s capacity plan. So 5 sessions churning subscribe centres saturate the 0.8 req/s adsb.fi bucket (config.py:52). The budget arithmetic: budget_adsb_fi=40000 (config.py:43), and hot stops at 40000-(8640+1000) (demand.py:400), so the hot share is 30,360. At about 0.8 req/s that lasts roughly 10.5 h. After that, focus has only the 1,000-call reserve left. The day key rolls over at UTC midnight (budget.py:37-38), so every user sees throttled/'daily budget share exhausted' until 00:00 UTC. The per-host and collector-wide caps still hold, so no owner rule is broken. This is an amplified feature-level DoS. Heavy legitimate use (6 hot cells plus focus all day, about 0.4 req/s) can already approach the share, which limits the incremental impact to roughly 2-4x amplification.

findings.summary: The /api/v1/ships ETag is built only from ShipStore.version, but the body's meta (stale, lag, meta.ais connected/gap_open_since/heartbeat_stale) depends on the clock and on the AIS status. When the AIS feed stops, the version stops changing, so every revalidation gets a 304 and the client keeps showing the old 'fresh/connected' meta indefinitely.
findings.failure_scenario:
1. A REST consumer fetches /api/v1/ships?bbox=… while AIS is healthy and gets meta.stale=false and ais.connected=true with ETag "s123".
2. The ais container disconnects and the gap stays open. No `ships` messages arrive, so ShipStore.version stays 123. ShipSweeper is frozen (inputDown), so there are no removals either.
3. Every 10 s the client revalidates with If-None-Match "s123" and gets 304. It keeps displaying stale=false / connected=true for as long as the outage lasts, even though a fresh 200 would say stale=true and heartbeat_stale=true.
4. AircraftController avoids this by putting recheckAtMs in its ETag.
findings.suggested_fix: Put the time/status-dependent inputs in the ETag: for example, a stale bucket (fetchedAt + SHIPS_STALE_S crossed), AisStatus heartbeat freshness, gap_open_since and connected. Or skip the 304 short-circuit when meta would differ.
findings.evidence: ShipController.java:75 builds the ETag as "s"+version only, and line 77 returns 304 on a match. ShipStore.version rises only when the ship map changes, in apply (line 226) or expire (line 268). expire returns Change.NONE when inputDown (line 257), and ShipSweeper passes inputDown during an outage. The ais sink flush() (ais/sink.py:113-115) sends no XADD when nothing is dirty, so during a feed outage no `ships` messages arrive and the version is frozen. The 200 body contains Meta.of(...) with stale = lag > 60 s computed at request time (Meta.java:22) and ais.publicView(now) (line 91). Both change with time and status but are not in the ETag, so a conditional GET (for example a browser revalidating after the 10 s max-age) keeps getting 304 and keeps showing stale=false / connected=true. AircraftController:62 includes recheckAtMs in its ETag for exactly this reason. Impact is limited because the web app does not use /api/v1/ships; it only calls /ships/{mmsi} and /track, which have no ETag. So only external or public REST consumers are affected.

findings.summary: The track endpoint loads gaps with repo.gaps(start, end, 500), which sorts started_at ascending, so on busy days the newest gaps are silently dropped. Track lines are then not split at those gaps, and the response's `gaps` array is incomplete with no truncation flag (unlike /ais/gaps).
findings.failure_scenario:
1. ADR-014 measured frequent server-side drops on wide subscriptions (1 in 3 global connections cut at ~51 s). With reconnects every ~2–3 min, a 24 h window holds more than 500 closed gaps.
2. GET /api/v1/ships/{mmsi}/track?from=now-24h gets only the oldest 500 gaps.
3. split() never sees the later gaps, so segments are drawn as continuous lines across real AIS outages (any outage under 15 min is not caught by the time-jump rule).
4. `gaps` omits them, with no flag telling the client the list is partial.
findings.suggested_fix: Fetch the gaps that overlap the returned points without a hard LIMIT (the window is at most 24 h), or order DESC and add a `gaps_truncated` flag. When truncated, fall back to breaking the track conservatively.
findings.evidence: The code behaviour is as described. ShipRepository.gaps (lines 149-157) uses ORDER BY started_at LIMIT :lim, and ShipController.gapsWithOpen (line 212) calls it with GAPS_LIMIT=500. For a 24 h window with more than 500 closed gaps, the newest gaps are dropped. split() (lines 219-234) then joins points across those gaps (only a jump over 15 min forces a break), and the track response has no truncated flag for gaps, unlike /ais/gaps (line 194). The precondition is not established, though. The default subscription is East Asia (contract §B1), and ADR-014:7 measured frequent server cuts only for global subscriptions (1 of 3 connections cut at 51 s). Exceeding 500 gaps in 24 h needs a disconnect about every 172 s all day. That is reachable only with a persistently flapping feed; for example, a global bbox cut at 51 s every time, with backoff never resetting (it needs 60 s healthy), gives a cycle of about 111 s and about 778 gaps/day. The default 6 h window would need a gap every 43 s. The consequence is also mild: lines drawn across short (seconds to 60 s) reconnect gaps in the newest part of the track.

findings.summary: The new wakeline_ais ACL user (and the collector user) can run CLIENT TRACKING in BCAST mode. This probably bypasses the key restriction the SCAN/RANDOMKEY deny was added to enforce: it would reveal key names such as wakeline:session:sessions:<id>, and the session ID is the ops login cookie.
findings.failure_scenario: COMMON is '+@all -@dangerous ...', and CLIENT TRACKING is @slow @connection, not @dangerous, so the ACL allows it. AIS_DENY only removes x*-group commands and scan/randomkey. The ais process parses attacker-controlled internet data, so assume it is compromised. It connects as wakeline_ais and sends `HELLO 3` then `CLIENT TRACKING ON BCAST` with no prefix. As far as I recall the Redis source, BCAST prefixes and RESP3 invalidation pushes are not checked against ACL key patterns, and resetchannels only covers pub/sub. If so, every time the api writes a session hash (login, or the lastAccessedTime update on each ops request), Redis pushes the key name wakeline:session:sessions:<sessionId> to the attacker. The attacker base64-encodes the ID into a WAKELINE_SESSION cookie and calls api:8000 directly on the internal network. CSRF is a double-submit cookie (CookieCsrfTokenRepository), so the attacker can set a matching WAKELINE_CSRF cookie and X-CSRF-Token header. Result: full ops access (settings, provider disable, audit). I could not run Redis here, so the claim that Redis 8 does not filter BCAST invalidations by ACL still needs to be confirmed with the proposed redis_acl_test case.
findings.suggested_fix: Add `-client|tracking` (and `-client|caching`) to COMMON, or at least to COLLECTOR_DENY and AIS_DENY. Then add `denied "CLIENT TRACKING BCAST" "${S[@]}" client tracking on bcast` and the same check for ${K[@]} to infra/tests/redis_acl_test.sh.
findings.evidence:
infra/redis/start.sh:29 COMMON='resetchannels +@all -@dangerous ...'. CLIENT TRACKING is in @connection/@slow, not @dangerous. AIS_DENY (line 40) = COLLECTOR_DENY (line 37), which removes only x*-group commands plus scan/randomkey, so client|tracking stays allowed for wakeline_ais and wakeline_collector. HELLO 3 is also allowed; infra/tests/redis_acl_test.sh:66 even asserts that HELLO 3 works under the same COMMON rules. The test file never checks tracking.

The key point is Redis source. On the 8.0, 8.2, 8.4 and 8.6 branches, tracking.c `sds trackingBuildBroadcastReply(client *c, rax *keys)` builds the BCAST invalidation array from every modified key and filters only NOLOOP. It has no ACL check. Only upstream `unstable` has since changed this to `trackingBuildBroadcastReply(user *u, ...)` with `if (check_acl && ACLUserCheckKeyPerm(u, key, len, CMD_KEY_ACCESS) != ACL_OK) continue;`. That fix confirms the bypass was real, and no released 8.x branch has it. The pinned image is redis:8-alpine.

The rest of the chain holds:
- Session keys are `wakeline:session:sessions:<id>` (application.yml `data.redis.namespace: wakeline:session`).
- DefaultCookieSerializer (SecurityConfig.java:93-100) keeps the default base64 encoding of the ID in WAKELINE_SESSION.
- CSRF is CookieCsrfTokenRepository double-submit (SecurityConfig.java:83-89), so an attacker can set a matching WAKELINE_CSRF cookie and X-CSRF-Token header.
- No origin, IP or fingerprint binding exists on ops endpoints.
- ais shares the single `wakeline` bridge network with api, which exposes 8000 (compose.yml:230-231, 135).

The repo's own threat model at start.sh:36 treats key-name leakage to a compromised collector/ais as session theft. That is why SCAN and RANDOMKEY are denied, and this is a parallel path that is left open. Severity stays medium because it first requires compromise of the ais or collector process.

I did not run Redis. This is verified from the upstream source of the release branches.

findings.summary: The selected ship's track gap list keeps an open gap (ended_at null) forever. After the AIS outage ends, every later live observation starts a new one-point segment, and the map draws a dashed 'AIS 공백 hh:mm–hh:mm' link between every pair of points.
findings.failure_scenario: A ship is selected. The AIS connection drops, so status.sources.ais.gap_open_since = X. During the outage the user pans or zooms, or the tab resumes. The server force-resends ship_selected, and the shipSelected effect calls mergeAisGaps, which pushes {started_at:X, ended_at:null}. The same thing happens if the ship is selected during the outage: the REST /track gaps from gapsWithOpen include the open gap, and finish() merges it too. When the gap closes, mergeAisGaps adds {X, Y} as a separate entry, because the dedupe compares ended_at. The stale {X, null} entry is never removed or replaced. In gapBetween (lib/ships.ts:426) an ended_at of null means Infinity, so for every later point gapBetween(lastEnd, p.ts) is true and appendShipTrack pushes a new single-point segment. I reproduced this with a scratch vitest: 5 appends after a closed gap produced 6 segments. shipTrackFeatures then emits a gray dashed 'AIS 공백 …' feature with a label between every consecutive 60 s observation, falsely claiming AIS outages. This lasts until the user reselects and can grow to thousands of labelled gap features. If the gap was open when the track loaded, ShipCard also keeps listing it as '진행 중' (still ongoing), because shipTrack.gaps is copied only in finish().
findings.suggested_fix: Treat an open gap as a placeholder for its started_at. When a closed gap with the same started_at arrives, or gap_open_since becomes null, replace or drop the open entry in mergeAisGaps, in shipTrackFromRest's gap list, and in setData({shipTrack}). Alternatively rebuild track.gaps from the current status on each merge rather than only appending.
findings.evidence:
MapView.tsx:41-49: mergeAisGaps pushes {started_at:X, ended_at:null} whenever status.ais.gap_open_since is set. Dedupe compares started_at AND ended_at (line 45), and nothing ever removes or replaces the open entry. It is called from finish() (line 504, when a ship is selected during an outage) and from the ship_selected effect (line 526). The server force-resends ship_selected on every initial set (ShipFanout.onInitial calls selected(), which sets shipSelectedForce), i.e. on subscribe (pan/zoom) and resume.

After the outage closes, last_gap {X,Y} is appended as a separate entry. ships.ts:423-429 gapBetween treats ended_at null as Infinity. appendShipTrack (ships.ts:495) therefore starts a new segment for every later point, and shipTrackFeatures (ships.ts:528) labels every link 'AIS 공백'.

I reproduced this with a scratch vitest run against the real lib/ships.ts, using gaps [{X,null},{X,Y}] and 5 appends at 60 s spacing after Y. The result was segs=6 and gap labels ['AIS 공백 00:59–01:06','AIS 공백 01:06–01:07','AIS 공백 01:07–01:08','AIS 공백 01:08–01:09','AIS 공백 01:09–01:10']: false outage claims between consecutive live observations. They persist until the user reselects (gaps cap at 200 entries, but the {X,null} entry is never evicted by closure).

findings.summary: When no aisstream key is configured, the status bar permanently shows a red 'AIS 끊김' badge with the tooltip '재연결 중(지수 백오프)' (reconnecting with exponential backoff). No reconnect is happening: the ais process is intentionally disabled.
findings.failure_scenario: `aisstream_key=` is empty, which is the documented 'ships layer off' configuration in .env.example. ais/main.py calls feed.on_disabled(): state='disabled', and the sink writes connected='0' with a fresh updated_at every 5 s. AisStatus.publicView (apps/api/.../AisStatus.java:104) reports connected=false and never exposes `state`. aisBadge sees connected === false and returns {text:'AIS 끊김', tone:'bad', title:'… 재연결 중(지수 백오프)'}. Every viewer sees a red outage badge and a false reconnecting claim indefinitely. The ais health check even says the disabled state is shown on screen ('상태 해시·화면에 이유가 보인다'), but it is not. Turning the ships layer on also shows '선박 수신 대기' (waiting for ships) forever, with no reason given.
findings.suggested_fix: Expose the collector state in status.sources.ais (e.g. state: 'disabled'). In aisBadge, render a neutral 'AIS 꺼짐 · 키 없음' (AIS off, no key) or hide the badge when state === 'disabled', and only say '재연결 중' when state is connecting or backoff.
findings.evidence:
.env.example:44-45 documents `aisstream_key=` (empty) as 'ships layer off'. ais/main.py:109-111 then calls feed.on_disabled(), which sets state='disabled' (feed.py:164-167) and leaves connected False. The sink still runs and writes the status hash every 5 s (sink.py:240-255) with connected '0' (sink.py:183) and a fresh updated_at.

AisStatus.parse reads `state` (AisStatus.java:80), but publicView (lines 104-127) never emits it. It puts connected=f.connectedNow() = false because the heartbeat is fresh, and f.present()=true, so the view is not null. StatusService.java:105 puts this in status.sources.ais.

web ships.ts:379: `if (ais.connected === false) return {text:'AIS 끊김', tone:'bad', title:'… 재연결 중(지수 백오프)'}`. StatusBar.tsx:27,48 renders it for every viewer. The result is a permanent red outage badge with a false claim that reconnection is in progress. It also contradicts ais/health.py:6, which says disabled is a configuration state whose reason is shown on screen.

findings.summary: Position source is shown as 'GNSS(선박 보고)' (GNSS, reported by the ship) even when the ship never reported it. The collector maps AIS Timestamp 60 ('not available', the default) and a missing Timestamp to 'gnss' (apps/collector/wakeline_collector/ais/parse.py:295). The web label then presents that guess as ship-reported data.
findings.failure_scenario: A Class A or Class B position report arrives with Timestamp=60 (ITU/USCG: time stamp not available, default) or with no Timestamp field. parse.py does `POSITION_SOURCE.get(ts, 'gnss') if ts is not None else 'gnss'`, so position_source='gnss'. ShipCard's '위치 출처' (position source) row renders POSITION_SOURCE_LABEL.gnss = 'GNSS(선박 보고)'. The ship said nothing about its fix source; the value is a heuristic fill-in, which violates the rule that unknown values are shown as '—'. Even for Timestamp 0–59 the field only means an electronic position-fixing system (EPFS) produced the fix, not specifically GNSS; the schema itself says '장치 종류는 단정하지 않는다' (the device type is not asserted).
findings.suggested_fix: In parse.py, emit null for Timestamp 60, missing or out-of-range values, and allow null in schemas/ship_state.v1.json and in ShipState/ShipLite. In the web, show '—' for null and relabel gnss as '전자 위치 장치(EPFS) 보고' (reported by an electronic position-fixing system) rather than 'GNSS'.
findings.evidence:
parse.py:283 `ts = _int(body.get('Timestamp'))`. parse.py:295 `position_source=POSITION_SOURCE.get(ts, 'gnss') if ts is not None else 'gnss'` with POSITION_SOURCE = {61,62,63} (line 35). Timestamp 60, which is the default 'time stamp not available' value, and a missing Timestamp therefore both become 'gnss'.

ShipCard.tsx:80 shows POSITION_SOURCE_LABEL.gnss = 'GNSS(선박 보고)' (ships.ts:309). That asserts both GNSS and 'reported by ship'. The repo's own schema (schemas/ship_state.v1.json position_source) says '장치 종류는 단정하지 않는다' (the device type is not asserted).

In the checked-in real fixture (fixtures/ais_east_asia_90s.jsonl), 10 of 428 position reports (~2.3%) carry Timestamp=60, so the case does happen.

Mitigation: change-contract-v2.md:47 (binding) explicitly specifies 'else "gnss"', so the collector follows the contract. The concrete honesty defect is mainly the UI wording and the 60→gnss fill-in, which the owner rule forbids. That makes it low severity, and the fix also needs a contract amendment.

findings.summary: Turning the aircraft layer off now stops the server from sending aircraft snapshots and diffs. The client still keeps aircraftStates and aircraftCount, so the status bar keeps showing a frozen 'aircraft N' count as if it were current.
findings.failure_scenario: The user switches the aircraft layer off (layers {aircraft:false}). WsHub.runFanout and sendInitialSet skip aircraft for that session. setLayers only handles ships and never clears aircraftStates or updates aircraftCount. The user pans to a different region or waits 30 minutes, and StatusBar (StatusBar.tsx:37, tooltip '현재 지도 영역(구독 bbox) 안의 항공기 수', 'aircraft in the current map area') still shows the old bbox's count. Search and alert helpers also keep reading those frozen aircraftStates.
findings.suggested_fix: When aircraft is switched off in setLayers, clear aircraftStates, post an empty snapshot to the worker, and set aircraftCount to null. StatusBar should then render '—' while the layer is off.
findings.evidence:
ws.ts:237-248 setLayers resets ship state only when ships change. For aircraft it only sends {type:'layers'}. The server then skips aircraft: WsHub.java:411-416 (sendInitialSet clears s.sent/seq when layerAircraft is false) and 452-453 (runFanout sends no snapshot/diff).

aircraftCount is set only in the snapshot/diff handlers (ws.ts:373, 388), and aircraftStates is cleared only on snapshot or in resetData (a test helper, store.ts:114-118). StatusBar.tsx:36-37 renders `aircraft {s.aircraftCount}` unconditionally with the tooltip '현재 지도 영역(구독 bbox) 안의 항공기 수' (aircraft in the current map area). After the toggle and a pan, it shows the old bbox's count as current.

The frozen aircraftStates also feed predictionTargets (MapView.tsx:148, maplayers.ts:225-236). Alerts keep arriving, so prediction lines for PREDICTED alerts are drawn from stale states. AircraftSearch.tsx:68 also flies to a stale position. The impact is display-only, so severity is low.

findings.summary: The new AIS chaos scenario disconnects the ais container from the compose network but has no trap to reconnect it. Interrupting the script during the cut leaves ais detached indefinitely, even across `docker restart`.
findings.failure_scenario: The operator runs `tools/chaos.sh ais` and presses Ctrl-C, or the shell is killed, during `sleep "$AIS_CUT_S"` (60 s by default). `docker network disconnect` has already removed the network from the container's config, and no EXIT/INT trap runs `docker network connect`. The ais container stays offline: it cannot reach aisstream or Redis, its health check fails, and unhealthy does not trigger a restart. `docker restart` does not reattach it and `make up` does not either. Ship data silently stops until someone reconnects it by hand or recreates the stack.
findings.suggested_fix: After the disconnect, install `trap 'docker network connect --alias ais "$NET" "$A" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true' EXIT INT TERM`, like the restore trap in `make bench`, and clear the trap after the normal reconnect.
findings.evidence:
tools/chaos.sh has no `trap` anywhere (grep finds none). Line 109 runs `docker network disconnect "$NET" "$A"`, then line 111 `sleep "$AIS_CUT_S"` (60 s by default), and only line 113 reconnects. The script uses `set -uo pipefail` without handlers, so Ctrl-C or SIGTERM during the sleep exits and leaves ais detached. docker network disconnect persists across `docker restart`.

The ais process does not exit when Redis or aisstream are unreachable: the sink catches RedisError (sink.py:256-260) and the client backs off, so restart: unless-stopped never recreates it. It stays detached until manual intervention.

The claim overstates one part: recent Compose v2 (checkExpectedNetworks in mustRecreate) recreates a running container that is missing its expected network, so `make up` likely does repair it.

The pre-existing db scenario (lines 86-89, docker stop then sleep 35) has the same untrapped pattern. This is an operator-tool robustness issue, so severity is low.
